description: Local study-topic knowledge base for the campus study assistant. Answers are short, general study explanations, not exam answers for a specific paper.

topics.answer: The Pomodoro technique is: study for 25 minutes with no phone, take a 5-minute break, and repeat. After 4 rounds, take a longer 15–30 minute break. It works because short, timed blocks make starting easier and breaks stop fatigue from building up. Try it for one subject first, and keep a small list of distractions to check only during breaks.
topics.title: Pomodoro technique

topics.answer: To beat procrastination, shrink the first step: instead of 'revise physics', write 'read page 1 and write 3 bullet points'. Set a 10-minute timer and allow yourself to stop after it — most people keep going once started. Put your phone in another room, and plan the next session the night before so you do not have to decide when tired.
topics.title: Beating procrastination

topics.answer: Effective revision is active, not just re-reading. Try: 1) Read a section, close the book, and write what you remember. 2) Test yourself with flashcards or past questions. 3) Space it out — review after 1 day, then 3 days, then a week. 4) Mix topics instead of doing one subject for hours. Short, tested recall beats long, passive re-reading.
topics.title: Effective revision

topics.answer: A simple exam plan: 1) List every topic and rate it weak, okay, or strong. 2) Spend most time on weak topics, with short reviews of strong ones. 3) Do timed practice questions under exam conditions. 4) The day before, review summaries only — do not learn new material late at night. 5) Sleep well; a rested brain recalls far better than a tired one.
topics.title: Exam preparation plan

topics.answer: Good notes are short and in your own words. Use headings, bullet points, and one example per idea. Leave space to add questions later. After class, spend 10 minutes cleaning them up and writing a 3-line summary at the top — that summary is what you will revise from. Avoid copying slides word for word.
topics.title: Taking good notes

topics.answer: In algebra, solve an equation by doing the same operation to both sides until x is alone. Example: 2x + 6 = 14 → subtract 6 from both sides: 2x = 8 → divide by 2: x = 4. For a quadratic like x² − 5x + 6 = 0, factor it as (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3. Always check your answer by putting it back into the original equation.
topics.title: Algebra basics

topics.answer: A derivative measures how fast a function changes — it is the slope of its graph at a point. Power rule: if f(x) = xⁿ, then f′(x) = n·xⁿ⁻¹. Example: f(x) = x³ gives f′(x) = 3x². The derivative of a constant is 0, and the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. If a question asks for a maximum or minimum, set the derivative equal to 0 and test the points around it.
topics.title: Calculus: derivatives

topics.answer: Pythagoras' theorem applies to right-angled triangles: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle). Example: sides 3 and 4 give 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = √25 = 5. Use it to find a missing side, and check that the longest side is always c.
topics.title: Pythagoras theorem

topics.answer: Newton's three laws: 1) Inertia — an object stays at rest or in steady motion unless a force acts on it. 2) F = ma — force equals mass × acceleration, so a bigger force or smaller mass gives more acceleration. 3) Action–reaction — every force has an equal and opposite force. Example: you push on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward when you walk.
topics.title: Newton's laws of motion

topics.answer: Energy is the ability to do work and is measured in joules. Kinetic energy (movement) is KE = ½mv². Gravitational potential energy is PE = mgh, where m is mass, g is about 9.8 m/s², and h is height. Energy is conserved: it changes form (for example, potential to kinetic as something falls) but the total stays the same in a closed system.
topics.title: Energy and work in physics

topics.answer: In a circuit, voltage (V, in volts) pushes current (I, in amps) through a resistance (R, in ohms). Ohm's law: V = IR. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere but voltage is shared; in a parallel circuit the voltage is the same across each branch but current splits. A common mistake is mixing up current (flow) with voltage (push) — keep their units straight.
topics.title: Electric circuits basics

topics.answer: A variable is a named box that stores a value, for example: name = "Ayesha" or age = 20. Common data types are integers (whole numbers), floats (decimals), strings (text), and booleans (True/False). Choose clear names like total_marks instead of x when the meaning matters, and remember that in most languages a string "20" and a number 20 are not the same thing.
topics.title: Programming: variables and data types

topics.answer: A loop repeats code without writing it again. A for loop repeats a set number of times, for example: for i in range(5): print(i) prints 0 to 4. A while loop repeats while a condition is true, so it must change something inside the loop or it will run forever. Use for when you know how many times, and while when you are waiting for a condition to change.
topics.title: Programming: loops

topics.answer: A function is a reusable block of code that does one job. Example in Python: def add(a, b): return a + b. Parameters (a, b) are the inputs the function expects; arguments are the actual values you pass when you call it, like add(3, 4). Return sends a result back to the caller — printing inside a function is not the same as returning a value you can use later.
topics.title: Programming: functions

topics.answer: The cell is the basic unit of life. Key parts: the nucleus holds DNA and controls the cell, mitochondria release energy from food (they are often called the powerhouse of the cell), the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves, and ribosomes make proteins. Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large vacuole.
topics.title: Biology: the cell

topics.answer: Photosynthesis is how plants make food using sunlight. The word equation is: carbon dioxide + water → (light, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen. It happens in chloroplasts, in the green pigment chlorophyll. The glucose is used for energy and growth, and the oxygen is released into the air. The rate increases with light intensity up to a point, then levels off.
topics.title: Biology: photosynthesis

topics.answer: DNA is a double-helix molecule that stores genetic instructions. It is made of four bases: adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G). A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. DNA is copied before a cell divides so each new cell gets a full set of instructions.
topics.title: Biology: DNA

topics.answer: The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number (number of protons). Rows are periods and columns are groups; elements in the same group have similar properties because they have the same number of outer electrons. Metals are on the left, non-metals on the right. An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons around it; the atomic number tells you the number of protons.
topics.title: Chemistry: periodic table

topics.answer: Acids have a pH below 7 and bases (alkalis in solution) have a pH above 7; pH 7 is neutral. An acid reacting with a base gives a salt plus water — this is neutralisation. Example: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water. Common lab indicators: litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali.
topics.title: Chemistry: acids and bases

topics.answer: A strong essay has: an introduction that states your main argument, body paragraphs that each make one point with evidence, and a conclusion that sums up without adding new points. Start each paragraph with a clear topic sentence. Draft first for ideas, then edit for clarity, and leave time to proofread — reading aloud catches mistakes your eyes skip.
topics.title: Writing essays and assignments

topics.answer: For a good presentation: keep slides short (a few words per slide, not paragraphs), speak to the audience rather than reading the screen, and practise aloud at least twice with a timer. If you forget a line, pause and look at your next heading — a short pause feels much longer to you than to the audience. Finish by restating your main point.
topics.title: Giving presentations

topics.answer: Sleep is part of studying, not a break from it: the brain consolidates memories during sleep, especially deep sleep. An all-nighter usually hurts recall the next day more than the extra hours help. Aim for a regular sleep time, stop screens 30 minutes before bed, and review your hardest topic briefly before sleeping — then let sleep do its job.
topics.title: Sleep and memory
